reader.title: Killing of Eli Williams
bases: An unidentified person fired a single pistol shot from outside a Black church and killed the preacher; no mob, band, posse or officers are reported, and no motive is given (A1, A10, A7).
Every report is a copy or condensation of one press-wire dispatch (A1, A2, A10, A7, A8); no local Alabama report, inquest or follow-up was found, so there is no independent second account.

summary.text: The killing of Eli Williams was the fatal shooting of a Black preacher in his pulpit during Sunday services at a church near Mitchell Station, Alabama, on July 28, 1895.
The gunman, believed to have fired from outside the building, was never identified in the coverage, and two Black men standing outside were held only as witnesses.
The story circulated nationally as a short wire item under headlines such as "Assassinated in the Pulpit."
Services were under way in a "negro church" near Mitchell Station on Sunday when a pistol shot rang out.
The preacher, the Rev. Eli Williams, described in one version as the pastor of the church, fell dead in the pulpit with the ball in his heart.
According to the dispatch, the assassin was believed to have stood outside the church when he fired, and his identity was not known.
A condensed version put it more bluntly: "There is no clew to the assassin."
Two Black men, Swing and Pleasant McKee, who had been standing outside the church, were arrested.
The dispatch stressed that they were held "simply as witnesses," not as suspects.
No report of an inquest, of any other arrest, of a motive or of a trial appears in the coverage, and no local Alabama account was found.

The episode reached readers almost entirely through a single wire dispatch datelined Mitchell Station, which appeared on July 29 in the Topeka State Journal, the Alexandria Gazette and the Deseret Evening News of Salt Lake City.
The Providence News and the Santa Fe Daily New Mexican carried it the same day, as did the San Antonio Daily Light in a garbled form.
Shorter versions followed in Ohio and Arizona weeklies on July 31 and in a Wisconsin column of "Waifs from the Wires" on August 1.
The Kansas State Ledger printed the fullest text on August 2, and the Leavenworth Herald reduced it to one line in its "News in Brief" on August 3.
Headlines centered on the pulpit setting, as in the Topeka State Journal's "SHOT WHILE PREACHING. A Negro Minister Killed While Standing in His Pulpit." and the Ohio Democrat's "Shot In the Pulpit."
The papers identified the church and the minister by race but offered no comment on motive and no editorial remark.
No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press.
Telegraphic copies varied on basic details.
The San Antonio Daily Light datelined the story "Mitchell Station, W. Va." and named the preacher "Rev. W. E. Lewis," while the Arizona Weekly Journal-Miner placed it at "Mitchell's Landing, La."
Because every other copy, including the fullest versions, gives Eli Williams and Alabama, those variants are most likely transmission errors.

accounts.label: Wire report (Mitchell Station dispatch)
accounts.gist: During Sunday services in a negro church near Mitchell Station, Ala., a pistol shot killed the preacher Eli Williams in his pulpit; the unknown assassin was thought to have fired from outside, and two Black men standing outside were held as witnesses.

accounts.label: Variant wire copy (San Antonio)
accounts.gist: The same story datelined Mitchell Station, W. Va., with the preacher named Rev. W. E. Lewis.

framing.detail: Papers ran the dispatch as a brief under headlines such as 'SHOT WHILE PREACHING. A Negro Minister Killed While Standing in His Pulpit.' and 'Assassinated in the Pulpit.', identifying the church and victim by race and offering no motive or comment.

conflicts.note: Only the San Antonio copy gives 'W. E. Lewis'; every other copy, including the fullest, names Eli Williams, so 'Lewis' is most likely a telegraphic or editing error.
The W. Va. and La. datelines each appear in one copy of otherwise identical text and are probably wire or typesetting errors; most copies say Alabama.
The wire copies speak of a single assassin; one brief (A11, a reprint) says 'unknown assassins'.

Swing and Pleasant McKee, two negroes, who were standing outside, were arrested. They are held, however, simply as witnesses.
